📊 Alibaba previews Qwen4 architecture

Alibaba released Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, an open multimodal model and early preview of the architecture planned for Qwen4. It has 125B parameters, but uses only 6B for each text fragment. Another 51B sit in separate memory for frequent combinations.

The design keeps the model large while reducing compute. Alibaba says training is about 9 times cheaper than Qwen3.7-Plus, while the model already performs better on coding, tool-use tasks, and long office workflows.

Long-context support reaches 262,000 tokens by default and up to 1 million tokens in extended mode. At 1 million tokens, a new retrieval mechanism can significantly speed up processing. The weights are already open on Hugging Face.

🤖 OpenAI Previews Cloud-Based Codex

In an interview, Thibault, OpenAI’s head of Codex and ChatGPT, said the current Codex may look primitive in 2-3 months. Next-generation Astra-based agents will need the cloud, where they can run more parallel processes than a typical laptop can handle.

Agent speed is also expected to rise. Today’s Ultra Fast rate of 750+ tokens per second could become the default. Codex and ChatGPT will increasingly share one harness across coding and other tasks.

The stated end goal is Personal AGI, a single personalized app whose interface changes with the user’s task.

🗣 Bill Gates says AI has become a GLOBAL security threat.

The Microsoft founder is reportedly seeking a meeting with China's Xi Jinping later this year to push for international controls on the most dangerous AI models.

Gates urges countries to monitor whether AI can create molecules and carry out biological attacks. He believes China could restrict dangerous model releases if the U.S. acts first.

Recent tests involving AI systems from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta saw them hack real-world websites, incidents Gates says should "blow people's minds."

Time magazine recently released its 2026 list of “The 100 Most Influential People in AI.” The selection has drawn notice because several prominent leaders in the AI field are absent from the list.

Notable figures such as Jensen Huang, Sundar Pichai, Mark Zuckerberg, Lisa Su, Satya Nadella, Demis Hassabis, and Alex Karp are not included in this year’s ranking.

Time’s annual list highlights individuals recognized for their significant impact on artificial intelligence. The omission of these industry leaders represents a departure from expectations, given their established roles in shaping AI development and deployment.

Anthropic has launched the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a new way for AI systems like Claude to control robots and lab equipment using a single interface.

MHS provides a standard method for AI agents to communicate with various lab and factory devices, instead of using different programming interfaces. It uses common drivers to handle device commands, properties, and safety limits.

In the past, bringing different instruments into a lab or factory took a lot of time. MHS simplifies this by using easy read/write drivers and reference files that outline device features and safety guidelines.

AI agents can connect to devices through command-line interfaces or custom code, helping them manage tasks and adapt based on experimental results.

According to Anthropic, early projects have shown that integration times have dropped significantly, going from weeks to just hours or even minutes.

🧠 OpenAI expects AGI by the end of 2026

OpenAI may have just put a date on AGI. Sam Altman reportedly said OpenAI is “not quite yet” at AGI but expects the company to have an internal system he would call AGI by the end of this year.

OpenAI has apparently already hit its internal benchmark for an autonomous AI research intern.

That system, reportedly known internally as Astra, can take an experimental idea, implement it in OpenAI’s codebase, run the experiment and return the results or take a research paper and perform work that could previously keep a human researcher busy for a week.

Altman says Astra could enable “persistent agents” that work alongside people for extended periods.

But he believes the biggest impact will be AI discovering genuinely new knowledge and inventing things that matter.

A federal judge has blocked the Pentagon from blacklisting Anthropic, ruling that the action was “illegal and baseless.” 

Judge Rita Lin determined that there was no sufficient justification for labeling Anthropic as a supply-chain risk, a classification typically associated with threats like sabotage or system interference. The government tied its decision to Anthropic’s public criticism of Pentagon policies. 

The court found the Pentagon’s actions violated Anthropic’s First Amendment rights, failed to provide due process as required by the Fifth Amendment, and did not comply with statutory requirements. 

The case began after Anthropic declined to allow its Claude AI system for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous lethal warfare, despite Pentagon requests for broader operational use.

AI becomes a second pair of eyes in brain surgery 🧠

For the first time, surgeons in London have used AI during surgery to help remove an 11mm pituitary tumor pressing against the patient’s optic nerves.

Trained on hundreds of surgical videos, the AI highlighted hidden blood vessels and nerves in real time, helping surgeons identify safer areas to operate.

Professor Hani Marcus described it as a “second pair of eyes” but the final decisions always remain with the surgeon.

48-year-old Rhys Hibbert regained clear vision for the first time in a year, and his dizziness disappeared. The team now hopes to develop a fully functional AI surgical assistant and move toward larger clinical trials.
